note_on_method: Nobody working on this has played on these courts. Every claim below comes from a named source in `sources`, and because the Town of Cary states its court counts in prose rather than in a table, each count here is quoted in the words the town used. Two Cary venues with stated court counts are missing from this page on purpose, including the best-known one in town; the reason is in the FAQs rather than hidden. Where a source is silent — lighting at two of the three parks, surface everywhere — the note says so instead of filling the gap.

slots.parking: Cary publishes more about parking than most towns we have read, but only in one place. Carpenter Park's features list states "Parking for 30 Cars", which is the only capacity figure any operator in this directory has given us for a pickleball site — and thirty spaces for a sixteen-acre park with a playground, a community garden, pedestrian trails and three pickleball courts is worth knowing before you drive out on a Saturday. Neither of the other two parks states a capacity, a time limit, a permit requirement or a fee. Ed Yerha Park's page lists restrooms and a picnic shelter but says nothing about where to leave a car, and the Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway describes paved loop trails, a community garden and public art without mentioning parking at all. All three are neighbourhood parks where the courts share a site with playgrounds, shelters and, at McCrimmon, a reservable tennis court, so a space existing is not the same as a space being free when something else is on. Read the posted signs, and tell us what you find.
slots.peak_hours: The single most useful fact about timing in Cary is that two of these three parks close at dusk. Ed Yerha Park publishes its hours as "Sunrise to Sunset" flatly, with no extension. Carpenter Park and the McCrimmon Parkway park use the same longer formula — sunrise to sunset, extended in lighted areas where visitors are taking part in an approved extended-use activity until thirty minutes after it ends or 11 p.m., whichever comes first — which is a rule about organised activities, not an invitation to play late. Only McCrimmon has lighting stated for its pickleball courts, so it is the only one of the three where an evening game is a published possibility rather than an assumption. Access differs too, and the town is specific about it. Ed Yerha's status board reads "Pickleball Courts Open - First Come, First Served". McCrimmon's features list marks its pickleball courts "Non-reservable, first-come, first-served" while the tennis court beside them is reservable sixteen hours ahead — so at that park the racquet sport that can be booked is not the one you came for, and nobody can have taken the pickleball courts before you arrived. Cary also runs open play on Monday evenings 7 to 9 p.m. at McCrimmon, and leagues that use those courts periodically.
slots.surface_condition: We have nothing, and we are not going to invent it. Not one of the three parks states a surface material for its pickleball courts, let alone a condition or a resurfacing date, so every venue on this page reads "Not verified yet" on surface. What the town does describe is the shape of the provision, which is a different thing but still worth having. Ed Yerha Park was built by enlarging existing multi-purpose slabs, and the town describes it as the home of "Cary's outdoor Pickleball courts". Carpenter Park's three courts are explicitly multi-sport, sharing their surface with basketball — "Multi-Sport Courts: Basketball & 3 Pickleball Courts" — so the lines under your feet are not all yours. McCrimmon's are described as pickleball courts in their own right, alongside a separate lighted tennis court, which makes them the only purpose-labelled pickleball courts on this page. None of that tells you whether a surface is cracked, faded or freshly done, and no Cary source we have read does either.
slots.local_scene: Cary takes pickleball more seriously than most towns its size, and says so publicly: it calls itself one of the country's premier destinations for the sport, and Cary Tennis Park hosts the Professional Pickleball Association tour. Around that sits a real municipal programme. Pickleball University runs instructional classes from beginner 101 through to tournament preparation at the 400 level, taught by IPTPA-certified instructors. There is a Cary Pickleball League in spring and summer, a Ladies' Ladder League in autumn and spring, and a Senior 55-plus mixed doubles ladder in summer. The town runs five one-day Royal Court tournaments a year with names it clearly enjoys — Queen of the Creek in March, Knights of the Round Creek Table in March, King & Queen of the Creek in May, King of the Creek in September, Dames of the Creekdom in October. Open play happens Sunday afternoons 3:30 to 5:30 at Cary Tennis Park and Monday evenings 7 to 9 at McCrimmon, with the paddle-in-line system familiar from everywhere else. Middle Creek Community Center hosts the Wake County Senior Games. Much of that programme runs at the two venues this page cannot publish, which is a gap worth knowing about rather than papering over.

best_for.heading: Best after work
best_for.text: The Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway, and by default rather than by a close contest. It is the only one of the three verified Cary parks whose pickleball courts the town describes as lighted, and it is the largest at six courts. It is also the site of Cary's Monday evening open play, 7 to 9 p.m. The courts are non-reservable and first-come, first-served, so nobody can book them out ahead of you — unlike the tennis court next to them, which can be reserved sixteen hours in advance.

best_for.heading: Best if you are new to the town
best_for.text: Ed Yerha Park, which the town describes as the home of Cary's outdoor pickleball courts and where the status board says the courts are open first-come, first-served. Three courts and restrooms on site. It closes at sunset with no extension published, so it is a daylight venue. Formerly White Oak Park, and still signposted that way in places — the town renamed it for a former councilmember.

best_for.heading: Best if you know what parking is like
best_for.text: Carpenter Park is the only venue in this entire directory whose operator publishes how many cars fit: "Parking for 30 Cars". Three pickleball courts, shared with basketball on multi-sport slabs, plus a restroom structure and a picnic shelter. No lighting is stated for the courts, so plan for daylight.

faqs.q: How many pickleball courts does Cary have?
faqs.a: We have verified 12, across three town parks: six at the Neighborhood Park on McCrimmon Parkway, three at Ed Yerha Park and three at Carpenter Park. That is not all of Cary's pickleball. The town also states four lighted courts at Cary Tennis Park and three indoor rental courts at Middle Creek Community Center, neither of which we publish — see below. Private clubs and neighbourhood facilities are not included, because none of them publishes a court count we can cite.

faqs.q: Why is Cary Tennis Park not on this page?
faqs.a: Because the town publishes no street address for it. That is the whole reason. Cary Tennis Park is the best-known racquet facility in the county, it hosts the Professional Pickleball Association tour, and the town states plainly that it has four lighted pickleball courts. We read its facility page, its pickleball page and its court reservations page and none of them prints an address. A venue does not get a page here without one, because an address is how a reader finds a place and how we tell two venues apart. It goes in the day the town publishes one, and we would rather be visibly incomplete than quietly approximate.

faqs.q: Is there indoor pickleball in Cary?
faqs.a: Yes, at Middle Creek Community Center, and we have not verified it as a venue. The town rents three courts in the South Gym at $10 per hour per court, or $15 with a ball machine, with a maximum of eight people per court — Thursday and Friday 2 to 5 p.m. and Saturday noon to 2 p.m. from March to October, and Thursday and Friday noon to 2 p.m. from November to February. Social play only, no private lessons for profit. As with Cary Tennis Park, no street address is published, so it does not publish here.

One of the three does. The McCrimmon Parkway park's features list heads its entry "Lighted Pickleball Courts". Ed Yerha Park and Carpenter Park say nothing either way about lighting on their courts, so we record lighting there as not verified rather than as absent — an unlit court and an unmentioned one are different things, and only one of them is a fact. Carpenter Park's hours note refers to "lighted areas" of the park in general, which is not a statement about the pickleball courts.

faqs.q: Can I book a court in Cary?
faqs.a: Not at the three parks on this page. McCrimmon's pickleball courts are marked non-reservable, first-come, first-served, and Ed Yerha's status board says the same. Reservations in Cary are a Cary Tennis Park and Middle Creek Community Center matter — $8 an hour for an outdoor court at the tennis park sixteen hours ahead, or free walk-up outside reservations, and $10 an hour per court indoors at Middle Creek.

faqs.q: Does it cost anything to play?
faqs.a: No fee is published for any of these three parks, and no source states that they are free either, so we record cost as not verified rather than guessing. The prices Cary does publish — $8 an hour at Cary Tennis Park, $10 an hour per court at Middle Creek — are for two venues that are not on this page.

faqs.q: What happened to White Oak Park?
faqs.a: It was renamed. Ed Yerha Park is the former White Oak Park, renamed for a councilmember who served from 2012 to 2022 and volunteered for Cary for more than two decades. The town's own park page still explains the change, and its open data still carries the old name on the same point, which is how we matched the two records to one place.
